questions.prompt: A therapist says, “There is a problem. Who caused this?” What should come first instead?
options: Decide who is at fault, then tell the rest of the team.
Ask what happened, what needs to happen now, what you can reasonably do, and whether management is needed.
Ignore the problem until someone else complains.
Gossip about it so everyone can choose a side.

questions.prompt: What does Zura Spa mean by a problem-solving mindset?
options: The therapist must personally solve every problem without help.
Problems should never happen if therapists are skilled.
When a problem occurs, the therapist stays calm, understands it, acts within their authority, communicates, escalates when needed, and helps move toward a solution.
The therapist should only massage well; operations are not their concern.

questions.prompt: Why is a problem-solving mindset part of professional competence at Zura Spa?
options: Because a therapist who massages well but responds poorly when something goes wrong can still damage the client experience.
Because it replaces the need for escalation.
Because it allows therapists to ignore accountability.
Because it means management never needs to be involved.

questions.prompt: A therapist notices a small issue and immediately starts arguing about who is to blame. What standard is being broken?
options: Problems should never be noticed early.
A problem should not automatically become an argument, blame game, gossip, or an excuse for poor service.
The therapist must always shout so others take it seriously.
Blame must come before any attempt to understand the facts.

questions.prompt: Which statement best matches the Zura Spa standard?
options: You must control every problem personally.
You may not control the problem, but you are responsible for how you respond to it.
If you did not cause the problem, you have no responsibility.
Only management is responsible for responses to problems.

title: SECTION B — POOR RESPONSES vs GOOD RESPONSES

questions.prompt: The towels are running low. Which response shows a problem-solving mindset?
options: “There is no towel. Nobody is doing anything.”
“It is reception’s fault.”
“We are running low on towels. I have informed the appropriate person, and for this session we can use the available clean set while more are prepared.”
Say nothing and hope the next therapist deals with it.

questions.prompt: A therapist sees that a room is not ready and says, “It is not my job,” then does nothing, including no communication. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing. Only housekeepers may speak about rooms.
There is a difference between not having authority to solve something and refusing to communicate or assist at all.
The therapist should have offered an unauthorized discount instead.
The therapist should have blamed the previous therapist in front of the client.

questions.prompt: A therapist becomes loud and insulting as soon as a scheduling mix-up appears. Why is this a poor response?
options: Anger as the first response usually makes the problem harder to solve.
Loudness is required so management notices.
Insults are acceptable if the therapist is stressed.
The client should hear every internal disagreement.

questions.prompt: Rather than reporting a broken massage gun through the proper channel, a therapist tells several colleagues about how “nobody maintains anything.” What is happening?
options: Correct escalation.
Gossip instead of escalation. The problem remains unresolved while tension spreads.
Good team communication.
Protecting the client experience.

questions.prompt: A therapist hides a client complaint because they are afraid of accountability. What is likely to happen?
options: The problem disappears.
Hidden problems usually become larger problems later.
Hiding complaints is required by Zura Spa.
The client will forget, so no action is needed.

questions.prompt: The massage room is not ready and the client is waiting. What is the first practical question?
options: “Who failed to clean it?”
“What needs to be done to make the room ready now?” Responsibility can be addressed afterwards.
“Which colleague can I blame publicly?”
“How do I get the client to leave?”

questions.prompt: Before acting, what should a therapist check?
options: Only who they dislike on the team.
What actually happened, who is involved, what has already been done, what is still required, and whether the client is affected.
Only rumours from other rooms.
Nothing. Assumptions are faster.

questions.prompt: How should urgency be decided?
options: By who shouts the loudest.
By client impact, safety, service disruption, and operational importance. A waiting client needs faster action than a non-urgent internal matter.
Every issue must go to management first, even a missing towel you can replace.
By which department you want to blame.

questions.prompt: A small spill is on the floor in a space you can safely clean, and it is within your responsibility. What should you do?
options: Wait for instructions for every basic situation.
Take reasonable action now, such as cleaning the spill.
Promise the client a refund.
Leave it so someone else can be blamed.

questions.prompt: Which report is more useful when the preferred room is still being cleaned?
options: “The room isn’t ready.”
“The preferred room is still being cleaned. We can use Room 2 now so the client is not delayed.”
“Management never prepares rooms.”
“I will change company policy on room assignment.”

questions.prompt: When should a therapist escalate?
options: Never. Escalation means you failed.
Only after gossiping with the whole floor.

When the issue involves client complaints, safety, money, refunds, discounts, harassment, serious conflict, equipment damage, policy decisions, injuries, serious misconduct, or anything outside the therapist’s authority.
For every missing towel, before trying any reasonable action.

questions.prompt: A problem occurs during a client’s session. How should the therapist protect the client experience?
options: Discuss internal blame in front of the client.
Stay professional, avoid arguing in front of the client, minimize disruption, and keep the client informed only as much as necessary.
Stop the massage and explain every internal failure in detail.
Carry unresolved anger into the next client’s session.

questions.prompt: A client asks for a discount because of a delay. What should the therapist not do?
options: Stay calm and escalate money, refunds, or discounts to the appropriate person.
Promise refunds, give unauthorized discounts, or make financial commitments for management.
Communicate the delay professionally.
Protect the client experience while the internal issue is handled.

questions.prompt: Why will Zura Spa not tolerate a pattern of poor problem-solving?
options: Because unexpected problems must never happen.

Unexpected problems will happen, but ignoring problems, constant complaining without solutions, hiding issues, acting outside authority, and letting internal issues affect clients cannot become acceptable.
Because therapists must solve every issue alone.
Because management wants no reports at all.

questions.prompt: How does a poor problem-solving mindset affect the team?
options: It only affects the individual therapist.
It can create extra work for others, frustration, blame culture, damaged trust, bigger conflicts, slower operations, and unnecessary burden on management.
It improves honesty because people hide fewer mistakes.
It has no effect if the massage technique is good.

questions.prompt: A colleague made a mistake preparing a room. What is the healthiest team approach?
options: Humiliate them in front of others so it never happens again.
Say “That is your problem” and refuse reasonable support.
Help protect the client, solve the immediate problem, then understand why it happened and prevent recurrence — without turning it into “Who can I blame?”
Hide the mistake so nobody feels uncomfortable.

questions.prompt: Does a solution-focused mindset mean mistakes should be ignored?
options: Yes. Accountability is unprofessional.
No. Generally: stabilize the situation, solve the immediate problem, understand the cause, address responsibility, then prevent recurrence.
Yes, if the client did not notice.
No. Blame the person first, then attend to the client.

questions.prompt: A therapist reports a problem and immediately walks away even though their involvement is still needed. What is missing?
options: Nothing. Reporting is always enough.
Resolve or hand over properly. Do not simply report and leave if your involvement is still necessary.
They should have offered an unauthorized refund first.
They should have posted the issue in a staff group chat for gossip.

questions.prompt: After a problem is handled, what should the therapist still do?
options: Forget it so nobody feels accountable.
Ask why it happened, whether it could happen again, what can change, and whether a process failed — so the team can learn.
Only remember who to blame next time.
Carry the anger into the next session.

questions.prompt: Which sequence matches the Zura Spa problem-solving standard?
options: BLAME → GOSSIP → HIDE → REPEAT
NOTICE → PAUSE → UNDERSTAND → PRIORITIZE → ACT → COMMUNICATE → ESCALATE → RESOLVE → LEARN
PANIC → SHOUT → PROMISE A REFUND → LEAVE
IGNORE → COMPLAIN → WAIT FOR SOMEONE ELSE
